sec.lead: How we protect your keys, your domains and your mail, what you are responsible for, and what we are still building.
sec.a.h: Secrets are never stored in the clear
sec.a.p: API keys are shown to you once, at the moment you create them, and stored only as a one-way hash. Even we cannot read a key back: if you lose it, you create a new one and revoke the old one. The DKIM private key of every domain is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, using a master key that is kept outside the database.
sec.a.b2: Keys carry a prefix, so they are easy to spot in logs
sec.a.b3: Every request is logged with the key that made it
sec.b.p: Every message is signed with DKIM and checked against your domain's SPF before it leaves. New accounts start in a sandbox that only allows sending to their own verified address, and every plan has daily and monthly limits. Addresses that bounce or complain go on a suppression list automatically, so a bad list cannot quietly damage your reputation, or the reputation of everyone who shares our infrastructure.
sec.b.b1: Sandbox until a domain is verified
sec.b.b2: Daily and monthly limits on every plan
sec.b.b3: Automatic suppression of bounces and complaints
sec.c.p: We keep message content and logs only for the retention period of your plan, then delete them. You can delete a domain or your account at any time and its data goes with it. We do not sell your data, we do not read your messages for advertising, and access to stored mail is limited to operating and protecting the service.
sec.c.b1: Retention from 1 to 30 days, depending on the plan
sec.c.b2: Deleting an account deletes its data
sec.c.b3: No advertising and no sale of data
sec.g.sub: Six things that are on by default.
sec.g0.p: DKIM private keys are encrypted at rest and only decrypted in memory when a message is signed.
sec.g1.p: Keys are stored as one-way hashes and shown once. A leaked database does not leak working keys.
sec.g2.p: The API and dashboard are served over HTTPS. Outgoing mail uses TLS whenever the receiving server supports it.
sec.g3.p: Sandbox for new accounts, rate limits and suppression lists keep spam out and deliverability high.
sec.g4.p: Message content and logs are deleted after the retention period of your plan.
sec.g5.p: Requests and delivery events are logged so you can see what happened and when.
sec.r.sub: Security works when both sides do their part.
sec.r1.b3: Tell you promptly about problems that affect you
sec.r2.b0: Keep API keys out of public code
sec.r2.b1: Use one key per app and revoke unused ones
sec.r2.b2: Send only to people who expect your mail
sec.r2.b3: Keep your DNS provider account secure
sec.q0.a: On servers we operate ourselves. Your messages are not passed to third-party analytics or advertising services.
sec.q1.a: Not yet, and we will not claim any certification before we actually hold it.
sec.q2.a: Message content is stored so it can appear in your dashboard and logs. Access to it is limited to running and protecting the service.
sec.q3.q: What if my API key leaks?
sec.q3.a: Revoke it in the dashboard and create a new one. Revoked keys stop working immediately.
sec.q4.q: How do I report a vulnerability?
sec.q4.a: Write to us through the contact page with as much detail as you can. We read every report and respond as soon as we can.
sen.lead: Transactional email from your own domain through one API call. Signed, queued, retried and fully logged, so you always know what happened to every message.
sen.a.p: Send a message with a single HTTP call and your API key. Geserd checks that the sender domain is verified, signs the message with DKIM and places it in the queue, so your application never waits for the receiving server to answer. The response contains an id that you can use to look up the message and its events at any time.
sen.a.b1: Plain JSON with HTML and text bodies
sen.a.b3: An id you can look up later
sen.b.p: Each email moves through clear states: queued, sent, delivered, bounced or complained. You see every step in the dashboard and receive the same events on your webhook. When a message bounces, the reason is shown in plain language, with the response of the receiving server attached, so you can decide what to fix instead of guessing.
sen.c.h: Retries, so a busy server does not lose your mail
sen.c.p: Receiving servers sometimes answer with a temporary error, for example when they are busy or when greylisting is active. Geserd keeps the message in the queue and tries again with growing delays instead of failing at once. Only permanent errors are treated as bounces, and those addresses are added to your suppression list so they are not tried again.
sen.c.b3: Failed addresses join your suppression list
sen.g.sub: What you get with every plan.
sen.g0.p: Every message is signed with a key generated for your domain.
sen.g1.p: Temporary failures are retried with growing delays.
sen.g2.p: Addresses that bounced or complained are skipped automatically.
sen.g3.p: Headers, body and delivery events are kept for the retention period of your plan.
sen.g4.p: Daily and monthly limits keep sending predictable and your reputation healthy.
sen.g5.p: New accounts send to their own verified address until a domain is verified.
sen.q0.q: Do I need my own domain?
sen.q0.a: Yes. You verify a domain you own by adding DNS records, then send from any address on it.
sen.q1.a: Yes, within a size limit that is listed in the API reference.
sen.q2.q: What happens when an address bounces?
sen.q2.a: It is added to your suppression list and future sends to it are skipped, so your bounce rate stays low.
sen.q3.a: The HTTP API comes first. SMTP credentials are planned for a later release.
rec.h1: Receive email. Reply in one call.
rec.lead: Point your MX at Geserd and every incoming message arrives as structured data on your webhook. Answer with the same API you use to send, and the conversation stays in one thread.
rec.a.h: Point MX. We do the rest.
rec.a.p: Add a single MX record and Geserd starts accepting mail for your domain. Each message is checked, parsed and stored, then shown in your dashboard and delivered to your server. Receiving works next to sending on the same domain: sending needs SPF and DKIM records, receiving needs an MX record, and the two never get in each other's way.
rec.a.b1: Works next to sending on the same domain
rec.a.b2: Headers, text, HTML and attachments parsed
rec.a.b3: Every message visible in the dashboard
rec.b.p: You never parse MIME yourself. When a message arrives, your endpoint receives clean JSON with the sender, the recipients, the subject and both the text and HTML bodies. If your server is down, Geserd retries the delivery, and the message stays safely stored in your inbox view either way.
rec.b.b1: Delivered to your webhook as it arrives
rec.b.b2: Retried when your server is down
rec.c.p: To answer a message, send a new email and set in_reply_to to the id of the message you received. Geserd adds the In-Reply-To and References headers for you, so mail clients group your answer with the original in a single conversation. Your reply goes through the same signing, queue, retries and logs as any other email.
rec.c.b3: Reply from any address on your domain
rec.g.sub: Receiving mail brings its own risks. We handle the boring and the dangerous parts.
rec.g0.p: Sender, recipients, subject, text, HTML and attachments as structured fields.
rec.g1.p: In-Reply-To and References are set so mail clients keep the conversation together.
rec.g2.p: Events are delivered with retries when your endpoint is unavailable.
rec.g3.p: Inbound volume limits per plan protect you and the platform from floods.
rec.g4.p: Search what arrived and when, with raw headers for debugging.
rec.g5.p: Attached files are stored with the message and reachable from the API.
rec.q0.q: Can I receive and send on the same domain?
rec.q0.a: Yes. Sending needs SPF and DKIM records, receiving needs an MX record. They do not conflict.
rec.q1.q: What if my webhook is down?
rec.q1.a: Delivery is retried, and the message stays stored in your inbox view either way.
rec.q2.a: Inbound limits apply to every account. Spam filtering is on the roadmap.
rec.q3.a: Yes, per plan. The pricing page lists the inbound volume of each plan.
dom.lead: Add your domain, publish a few DNS records and send and receive from any address on it. No mailbox limits, no per-address setup.
dom.a.p: The dashboard shows the precise DKIM, SPF and MX records for your domain, generated the moment you add it. Copy them into your DNS provider and press verify. There is nothing to guess and nothing generic: every value is specific to your domain and your account.
dom.b.h: From zero to sending in four steps
dom.b.p: Most domains are ready within minutes once the records have propagated. You add the domain, publish the records at your DNS provider, and verify. If a record is missing or wrong, the dashboard tells you exactly which one, instead of a generic failure.
dom.b.b1: Records generated the moment you add a domain
dom.b.b3: Re-check at any time after a DNS change
dom.c.p: We recommend sending from a subdomain such as mail.yourdomain.com instead of your root domain. This keeps the sending reputation of your transactional mail separate from your main domain, so a spike in bounces from one project never affects the other, and you can verify several subdomains independently.
dom.c.b3: Domain limits depend on your plan
dom.g.sub: Mailbox providers trust senders who prove who they are.
dom.g0.p: A 2048-bit key pair is generated for each domain. The private key never leaves the server.
dom.g1.p: One record authorizes Geserd to send for your domain.
dom.g2.p: We recommend a starting policy and explain how to tighten it over time.
dom.g3.p: Route inbound mail for the domain, or a subdomain, to Geserd.
dom.g4.p: Keep transactional mail on its own subdomain to protect your main domain.
dom.g5.p: Check your DNS again at any time after making changes.
dom.q0.a: We recommend it, for example mail.yourdomain.com. It keeps transactional reputation separate from your main domain.
dom.q1.a: No. You keep full control of your DNS and add the records at your own provider.
dom.q2.q: How many domains can I add?
dom.q2.a: It depends on your plan, from one on Free to ten on Business, and unlimited on Enterprise.
dom.q3.q: Can two accounts verify the same domain?
dom.q3.a: No. A domain can be verified by one account at a time.
hook.lead: Real-time events on your server for every delivery, bounce, complaint and incoming message, so your app can react without polling.
hook.a.p: Subscribe to the events you care about and ignore the rest. Every important moment in the life of a message, sent, delivered, bounced, complained, or a brand new message received, is available as a webhook event, so your app always knows the current state without asking.
hook.a.b3: Inbound and outbound events in one system
hook.b.p: Every event has the same envelope: a type, a timestamp and a data object that matches the type. There is no schema to memorize event by event, no deeply nested structures, just the fields you actually need to update your own database or notify a user.
hook.b.b1: Signed so you can verify the sender
hook.b.b3: Same format for inbound and outbound events
hook.c.h: Delivered even when your server is not
hook.c.p: If your endpoint returns an error or does not answer in time, Geserd retries the delivery with growing delays. You can see every attempt, its status code and the response your server sent, so debugging a missed webhook does not mean digging through your own logs first.
hook.g.sub: Webhooks are only useful if they actually arrive.
hook.g0.p: Failed deliveries are retried with growing delays.
hook.g1.p: Each request is signed with your endpoint secret so you can verify it came from us.
hook.g2.p: See every attempt, status code and response, right in the dashboard.
hook.g3.p: Only receive the event types you actually selected.
hook.g4.p: Send different events to different services, for example billing and support.
hook.g5.p: Endpoints must use HTTPS, so event data is never sent in the clear.
hook.q0.q: How do I verify a webhook?
hook.q0.a: Compare the signature header with an HMAC of the request body computed using your endpoint secret.
hook.q1.a: Any 2xx status means received. Any other response, or a timeout, is retried.
hook.q2.a: Every delivery attempt is logged. Manual replay from the dashboard is planned for a later release.
hook.q3.a: Yes. Respond quickly with a 2xx and process the work in the background of your own server.

bl.spf-dkim-dmarc.title: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, explained without the acronyms
bl.spf-dkim-dmarc.lead: Three records stand between your email and the spam folder. Here is what each one actually does, in plain language.
bl.bounces-and-suppression.title: Bounces, complaints and suppression lists, and why they matter
bl.bounces-and-suppression.lead: A high bounce rate is the fastest way to make every mailbox provider distrust your domain. Here is how Geserd tracks it and what you should do about it.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.spf.h: SPF: who is allowed to send
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.spf.p0: SPF, or Sender Policy Framework, is a DNS record that lists which servers are allowed to send email for your domain. When a receiving server gets a message claiming to be from yourdomain.com, it checks the SPF record for that domain and compares it against the server that actually sent the message. If the sending server is not on the list, the message looks suspicious, even if nothing else is wrong with it.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.spf.p1: An SPF record for Geserd looks like v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 ~all, meaning mail can come from that one IP address, and anything else should be treated with a soft fail rather than rejected outright. You only need one SPF record per domain, and if you already send mail from another provider, Geserd's IP needs to be added to the existing record rather than replacing it.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dkim.h: DKIM: proof the message was not altered
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dkim.p0: DKIM, or DomainKeys Identified Mail, adds a digital signature to every message using a private key that only the sending server holds. The receiving server looks up the matching public key in your DNS and checks that the signature still matches the message. If even a single character changed in transit, the signature breaks and the check fails.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dkim.p1: This is why Geserd generates a separate 2048-bit key pair for every domain you verify: the private key signs your outgoing mail, and the public key is published as a TXT record so any receiving server can verify it. You never handle the private key yourself, and it is encrypted at rest on our side, so a signature can only ever be produced by Geserd sending on your behalf.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dmarc.h: DMARC: what to do when a check fails
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dmarc.p0: SPF and DKIM can each fail independently without anyone being told. DMARC ties them together: it tells receiving servers what to do when a message claiming to be from your domain fails SPF, DKIM, or both, and it gives you an address to receive reports about it. A DMARC record with p=none asks servers to do nothing special yet, just report; p=quarantine asks them to send failing mail to spam; p=reject asks them to refuse it outright.
bp_spf-dkim-dmarc.dmarc.p1: We recommend starting with p=none so you can watch the reports for a few weeks and confirm every legitimate sending source, including Geserd, passes cleanly, before moving to quarantine and eventually reject. Tightening DMARC too early, before your setup is fully correct, is the most common way real customer email quietly disappears.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.hard.p0: A hard bounce means the receiving server permanently rejected the message, most often because the address does not exist. Continuing to send to an address like that after the first bounce does real damage: mailbox providers watch how often a sender keeps hitting invalid addresses, and treat it as a sign of a low-quality or purchased list, even if the rest of your sending is perfectly legitimate.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.hard.p1: This is why every hard bounce on Geserd adds the address to your suppression list automatically. The next time you try to send to it, the request still succeeds at the API level, but the message is not actually attempted, and the event log shows it was suppressed rather than sent.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.soft.h: Soft bounces get a second chance
bp_bounces-and-suppression.soft.p0: A soft bounce is temporary: a full mailbox, a server that is briefly down, or greylisting, where a receiving server intentionally delays first-time senders to filter out spam software that never retries. None of these mean the address is bad, so Geserd treats them differently from hard bounces and retries delivery with growing delays before giving up.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.soft.p1: Only after retries are exhausted does a soft bounce turn into a final failure in your logs, and even then the address is not suppressed, since the problem was very likely temporary rather than something wrong with the address itself.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.complaints.p0: A complaint happens when a recipient clicks "report spam" instead of unsubscribing or ignoring your message. Mailbox providers weigh complaints far more heavily than bounces, because a complaint means the mail was delivered successfully and a real person still did not want it. A complaint rate that creeps up, even from a small fraction of recipients, is often the first sign that a sending domain is about to lose trust.
bp_bounces-and-suppression.complaints.p1: Complaints are suppressed automatically on Geserd just like hard bounces, and they show up in your logs with the reason attached, so you can look at what was sent and to whom, and adjust your sending before the pattern repeats at a larger scale.

doc.qs.lead: Add a domain and send your first email in a few minutes.
doc.qs.p1a: In the dashboard, go to Domains and add the domain or subdomain you want to send and receive from. We recommend a subdomain such as mail.yourdomain.com to keep transactional reputation separate from your main domain.
doc.qs.p1b: The dashboard shows the exact DKIM, SPF and MX records for your domain. Add them at your DNS provider, then click verify. Most providers propagate changes within minutes, though it can occasionally take longer.
doc.qs.dnsnote: Most providers propagate DNS changes within minutes, though it can occasionally take longer.
doc.qs.p1c: In API keys, create a new key and store it somewhere safe. It is shown once, in full, at creation time, and never again after that.
doc.qs.p1d: Sending from a domain that is not verified yet is refused with the domain_not_verified error. Once verification succeeds, you can send to any address.
doc.qs.p1e: Point the MX record of your domain at your Geserd host and add a webhook endpoint in the dashboard. Incoming mail arrives at your endpoint as an email.received event, described in the API reference.
doc.err.lead: How Geserd reports problems, and what each error means.
doc.err.p2a: Every error response is JSON with an error field identifying the problem, and the HTTP status code reflects the category of failure: 4xx for something wrong with the request, 5xx for a problem on our side.
doc.err.row1: The action would exceed your plan's limit, for example the number of domains
doc.err.row1b: This action needs a dashboard session and cannot be done with an API key
doc.err.row2: The resource does not exist or does not belong to your account
doc.err.row3: A resource with this value already exists, for example a duplicate domain
doc.err.row4: The domain name is not a valid, syntactically correct domain
doc.err.row5: Too many requests in a short time; slow down and retry
doc.err.row6: Something failed on our side; safe to retry
doc.err.p2c: For 429 and 5xx responses, wait and retry with backoff. For 4xx responses other than 429, fix the request before retrying, since repeating the same invalid request will just fail again.
doc.rl.lead: How sending and receiving limits work, and what happens when you hit one.
doc.rl.p2a: Every plan has a monthly send limit and a daily send limit, plus a separate monthly inbound limit. Hitting the daily limit only blocks sending until the next day; hitting the monthly limit blocks sending until the plan resets or you upgrade. See the pricing page for the exact numbers per plan.
doc.rl.p2b: A send request that would exceed a limit is rejected before it is queued, so it never appears in your logs as attempted. Check the Usage page in Settings to see how close you are to each limit.
doc.rl.p2c: Independently of send limits, the API also limits how many requests per second a single API key can make, to protect the platform from accidental request loops. This limit is generous for normal use and only matters if a bug in your integration is retrying in a tight loop.

pr.sub: Start for free and scale as you grow.
pr.cta.p: Geserd gives small teams and solo developers a dependable way to send and receive email.
pr.paygo.d: Continue sending and receiving emails beyond your quota. Geserd charges your plan’s overage rate for each additional bucket of 1,000 emails. Available to paid subscriptions.
pr.add.dom.d: Your plan already comes with domains, but if you send from a separate one for each customer or brand, that number runs out quickly. This adds 10 more on top of it. Available on Pro and Business, and you can add or remove it yourself at any time. On Enterprise, the domain limit is set in your contract.
pr.add.ip.d: Available on request on the Business plan. A dedicated address keeps your sending reputation completely separate and under your control.
pr.q0.q: Do I need a credit card for Free?
pr.q0.a: No. Create an account and start sending on the Free plan without entering any payment details.
pr.q1.q: Why is the Free plan so small?
pr.q1.a: Free exists to let you verify a domain and test your integration end to end. Volume is kept small on purpose. For real sending, Pro is the intended step.
pr.q2.a: Every accepted send request counts toward the monthly and daily send limits. Received messages count toward the inbound limit separately.
pr.q3.a: Each message delivered to one of your verified domains and stored counts once, regardless of size or number of recipients. Messages rejected as spam before storage do not count.
pr.q4.q: What happens if I send more emails than my plan allows?
pr.q4.a: Without pay-as-you-go, sending returns an error until the period resets or you upgrade, and mail already queued is still delivered. With pay-as-you-go enabled on a paid plan, extra emails are billed at your overage rate.
pr.q5.a: Yes, at any time, up or down. A downgrade takes effect at the start of your next billing period.
pr.q6.q: What payment methods do you accept?
pr.q6.a: Billing is being finished during the beta. Cards will be supported first, with local payment methods for customers in Russia and neighbouring countries. Until billing opens, paid plans are not charged.
pr.q7.a: The Free plan has no time limit, so you can test as long as you like. If you need higher limits for a proof of concept, write to us and we will raise them temporarily.
pr.q8.q: Who can I contact about a custom plan?
pr.q8.a: Use the contact page and choose Enterprise. Tell us your expected volume and requirements, and we will reply with a proposal.
pr.note: Prices are shown in your region’s currency. Limits are indicative and may change during the beta.

ab2.lead: Geserd is one API for sending and receiving email from your own domain. Signed, delivered, logged, and yours.
ab2.s.p: Almost every project ends up rebuilding the same email plumbing, usually after something has already gone wrong in production.
ab2.s1.p: Records, DKIM, SPF, and a sender nobody trusts yet. Every project starts by rebuilding this.
ab2.s2.p: Without events you only find out about a bounce from an unhappy customer.
ab2.s3.p: Receiving means MX records, parsing and storage, so most teams skip it and lose the conversation.
ab2.s4.t: So it all sits behind one API
ab2.s4.p: Sending and receiving, both directions, with logs and webhooks included from day one.
ab2.m: One clear way beats five configurable ones. We say what works today and what does not. We keep our limits even when they are inconvenient, because deliverability is a promise to every sender.
ab2.l1.p: One request with an API key. You get an id back straight away, so every message can be traced.
ab2.l2.p: The message is signed with DKIM for your own domain, so receivers can check it really came from you.
ab2.l3.p: We hand it to the recipient’s server over an encrypted connection and wait for the answer.
ab2.l4.p: Delivered, delayed, bounced, complained. Each one lands in your logs together with the server’s own reply.
ab2.l5.p: Events are posted to your webhook, so your app can react the moment something changes.
ab2.b1.p: No reseller layer between your message and the inbox. Capacity grows as real usage grows, not before.
ab2.b3.p: English, Russian, German and French, including the emails we send you.
ab2.b4.p: We store only a hash, so we cannot read a key back and cannot leak it.
ab2.b5.p: Half price on paid plans for businesses in Siberian regions.
ab2.q0.a: A small independent team. We run the infrastructure ourselves rather than reselling someone else’s.
ab2.q1.a: Sending and receiving work today on the free plan. Paid checkout is still being connected, and the changelog tells you when it opens.
ab2.q2.a: The plans on the pricing page are current. If anything changes we announce it before it takes effect.
ab2.q3.a: Use the contact page. We read everything that comes in, including bug reports and rough edges you find.
hb.lead: How Geserd works, in plain words: what we believe, how we build, and how we look after you.
hb.why.p: Email is still the most reliable way to reach people, and still painful to set up. We exist to put signing, delivery, logs and inbound parsing behind one API so small teams can ship mail without becoming email experts.
hb.believe.p: One clear way beats five configurable ones. We say what works today and what does not. We keep limits even when they are inconvenient, because deliverability is a promise to every sender.
hb.run.p: We operate our own servers instead of reselling another email service. Capacity grows with real usage, and every plan has limits that protect sender reputation.
hb.ship.p: Every change that you can see or feel is written down in the public changelog with a date, in four languages. If it is not in the changelog, we did not announce it.
hb.incidents.p: Problems are posted on the status page as they happen, with their impact and current state. We update the entry until it is resolved and keep it visible afterwards.
hb.data.p: API keys are shown once and stored only as a hash. Mail travels over TLS and is signed with DKIM. You can export your data or delete your account yourself from the account page.
hb.help.p: Open a ticket from the dashboard or use the contact page. Replies arrive in the ticket and by email, in the language you picked.
hb.feedback.p: Bug reports and rough edges are the most useful thing you can send. The feedback card in the dashboard goes straight to us, and fixes land in the changelog.

fs.lead: One API call or plain SMTP delivers signed, queued and logged email from your own domain, and you can see what happened to every message.
fs.l.p: Each step is logged and sent to your webhook, so you never have to guess what happened. Pick an outcome to see its path.
fs.t.a1.p: You get an id back right away. Recipients that bounced or complained before are skipped.
fs.t.a2.p: The message is signed with DKIM and handed to the recipient’s mail server over TLS.
fs.t.a3.p: The receiving server accepts it. Your webhook hears about it within seconds.
fs.t.b3.p: A temporary problem, such as a full mailbox or a busy server. The message stays in the queue and is tried again.
fs.t.b4.p: The address does not exist or refuses mail. You get a bounce event with the reason, and the address can be added to your suppression list automatically.
fs.b1.p: Every message carries a DKIM signature for your domain, so receivers see mail from you, not from a shared sender.
fs.b2.p: Addresses that bounced or complained can be skipped automatically, which protects your reputation.
fs.b3.p: Fill templates with variables, add Reply-To, Cc, Bcc and custom headers.

fs.q1.q: What happens when an address bounces?

fs.q2.q: How do I connect software that only supports SMTP?
fs.q2.a: Use smtp.geserd.com on port 465 or 587, any username, and your API key as the password.

fr.q2.q: How large can an incoming message be?
fr.q2.a: Up to 10 MB including attachments. Anything larger is refused and the sender is told.

doc.bg.what-is-smtp.1: A postal system for the internet
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.2: Think of SMTP as the rules of the postal service. When you post a letter, you write the address on the envelope, drop it at a post office, and the post office passes it from sorting centre to sorting centre until it reaches the right door. SMTP does the same for email: the sending server writes who the message is from and who it is for, then passes it on until the receiving server accepts it.
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.4: Many programs that send email, such as online shop engines, website builders and newsletter tools, have a settings page that asks for an SMTP server, a port, a username and a password. That page is simply asking where to hand the message. Geserd gives you those four values, so the program can use us without any code.
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.7.0: Server: the address of the post office. For Geserd it is smtp.geserd.com.
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.7.1: Port: which door to use. Use 465 if the program offers “SSL” or “TLS”, and 587 if it offers “STARTTLS”. When in doubt, try 465 first.
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.7.2: Username and password: the username is a fixed word and the password is an API key that you create in the dashboard. Treat it like a password: anyone who has it can send mail as you.
doc.bg.what-is-smtp.8: The server name and the exact values for your account are also shown in the dashboard under SMTP, ready to copy.
doc.bg.dns-records.1: The address book of the internet
doc.bg.dns-records.2: Every domain has a list of small text entries called records. Other servers read them to learn where to deliver your mail and who may send it. You never see them in daily life, but they are the reason a message from your shop is believed or sent to spam.
doc.bg.dns-records.4.0: Type: what kind of information it holds. We use TXT (a piece of text) and MX (where mail is delivered).
doc.bg.dns-records.4.1: Name: which part of your domain it belongs to. @ means the domain itself, and a word such as _dmarc means a special place under it.
doc.bg.dns-records.4.2: Value: the content, usually a long line of letters. Copy it exactly, without adding spaces.
doc.bg.dns-records.5: The records Geserd asks you to add
doc.bg.dns-records.7: The first three are about trust and the last one is about receiving. The dashboard prints the real values for your domain, so you never type them from memory: you copy them from the screen.
doc.bg.dns-records.9: Open the DNS settings at the company where you bought the domain, create each record as shown, save, and press verify in the dashboard. Changes usually appear within minutes. The next guide shows each click.
doc.bg.add-dns.2.0: Know where the DNS lives. It is at the company that manages your domain. If you bought it at one place but moved the name servers to another, such as a website host, the records go to that second place.
doc.bg.add-dns.2.1: Open the Domains page in Geserd and leave it in a second tab. You will copy from it.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.0: Find the DNS page. Look for “DNS”, “DNS records”, “Zone editor” or “Name servers” in the domain’s settings.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.1: Press “Add record”. Choose the type exactly as Geserd shows it, TXT or MX.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.2: Fill in the name. Some companies want only the short name (_dmarc), others want the full name (_dmarc.yourshop.com). If one form is rejected, try the other. For the domain itself use @, or leave the field empty.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.3: Paste the value. Use the copy button in Geserd and paste. Do not retype it, and do not add quotation marks unless the form asks for them.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.4: Leave the lifetime (TTL) alone. The default, often called “Auto” or 3600, is fine.
doc.bg.add-dns.4.5: Save. Repeat for each record in the list, then return to Geserd and press verify.
doc.bg.add-dns.6.0: Two SPF records. A domain may have only one record starting with v=spf1. If you already have one from another service, add Geserd’s address to it instead of creating a second.
doc.bg.add-dns.6.1: A hidden space or line break at the end of the value. Paste again and check the end of the line.
doc.bg.add-dns.6.2: The domain name added twice. Some forms add .yourshop.com themselves, which turns the name into _dmarc.yourshop.com.yourshop.com. If verification fails, try the short name.
doc.bg.add-dns.8: Most companies publish a change within a few minutes. In rare cases it takes a few hours, and very rarely up to a day. If Geserd still shows a record as missing after an hour, open the record on your side, compare it character by character with the one in Geserd, and open a ticket if you cannot find a difference.
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.2: Anyone can type any address into the “From” line of an email, including yours. Without checks, criminals could send messages that look like they come from your shop. These three records are how the world’s mail servers tell real messages from fakes, and they are the biggest factor in whether your email reaches the inbox.
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.4: SPF is a guest list. It names the servers that are allowed to send mail for your domain. A receiving server looks at who actually delivered the message and checks the list. If the sender is not on it, the message looks suspicious.
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.5: DKIM: a seal that proves it was not changed
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.6: DKIM works like a wax seal on a letter. Geserd signs every message with a private key that only we hold. The matching public key lives in your DNS. The receiving server uses the public key to check the seal: if the message was altered on the way, the seal no longer fits.
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.7: DMARC: what to do when checks fail
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.8: DMARC is your instruction to the receiver. It says which of the two checks above must pass and what to do with a message that fails. The record Geserd gives you starts with p=none, which means “watch and report, do not block yet”. That is the safe way to begin. Later, once you are sure all your legitimate mail passes, you can ask receivers to treat failures more strictly.
doc.bg.dkim-spf-dmarc.9: You do not have to understand the details to benefit. Add the records Geserd shows, press verify, and the protection is in place.
doc.bg.first-email.2: Open Domains in the dashboard. A verified domain shows a green status. Sending from a domain that is not verified yet is refused with a clear message, so there is no risk of sending something by accident.
doc.bg.first-email.4: If you use a program that has SMTP settings, such as a shop engine or a website builder, paste the four values from the previous guide into its email settings, set the sender address to one on your verified domain, such as hello@yourshop.com, and use its “send a test email” button. The message should arrive within seconds.
doc.bg.first-email.6: If someone builds your site, you can hand them this example. They only need to replace the key and the addresses.
doc.bg.first-email.9: Open Logs in the dashboard. Every message appears with its state: accepted, delivered, or failed with the reason. If you do not see the message in your inbox, check the spam folder first, then the log.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.2: Open Logs and find the message. The status tells you where it stopped. “Delivered” means the other side accepted it, so look in the spam folder. “Failed” shows the reason in words, and “Bounced” means the address does not exist or the mailbox is full.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.4: Open Domains and press verify again. If any record shows as missing, go back to the DNS guide and compare it with the value in Geserd. Records can also disappear when someone changes the domain’s name servers, so check that the DNS page you edited is the one in use.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.6.0: Typos in the address are the most common cause of a bounce.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.6.1: Suppressed addresses. After repeated bounces or a spam complaint Geserd stops sending to an address to protect your reputation. You will see it in the suppression list.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.8: Short subjects without capital letters and exclamation marks, a clear sender name, a plain-text version next to the design, and an unsubscribe link in newsletters all help. Messages that are mostly an image, or that contain only a link, are often treated as spam.
doc.bg.troubleshooting.9: Still stuck? Open a ticket from the dashboard and include the message from the log. We will tell you what happened and what to change.

hb2.lead: How Geserd works, in plain words: what we believe, how we build, and how we look after you.
hb2.cta.h: Questions the handbook does not answer?
hb2.cta.p: Open a ticket or read the documentation: we answer in plain words.
hb2.why-we-exist.lead: Email is still the most reliable way to reach people, and still one of the most painful things to get right. Geserd exists to remove that pain.
hb2.why-we-exist.1: Every product that has users eventually needs to send email: a confirmation code, a receipt, a password reset, a notice that something happened. The first message is easy. The thousandth is where the trouble starts: it lands in spam, it bounces for a reason nobody can read, or it never leaves at all because a DNS record is wrong.
hb2.why-we-exist.2: Receiving is harder still. Most services stop at sending and leave replies to a separate mailbox, a separate tool and a separate set of rules. We think a conversation by email should be one thing: the message goes out from your domain, the reply comes back to the same place, and both travel over one API.
hb2.why-we-exist.3: What we are trying to do
hb2.why-we-exist.4.0: Make the first email take minutes. Add a domain, copy the records we show you, and send. Nothing else stands between you and a delivered message.
hb2.why-we-exist.4.1: Keep both directions in one place. Sending, receiving and replying use the same domain, the same keys and the same logs.
hb2.why-we-exist.4.2: Explain failures in plain words. When a message does not arrive, you should see why, not a code you have to look up.
hb2.why-we-exist.6: We build for small teams and solo developers who need email to simply work, and who do not have a person whose job is deliverability. If a product of yours sends a few hundred or a few hundred thousand messages a month, the service should feel the same: fast to set up, quiet while it runs, honest when something goes wrong.
hb2.why-we-exist.7: That is the whole reason. Everything else in this handbook is how we try to live up to it.
hb2.what-we-believe.lead: Beliefs are only useful if they change what we do on an ordinary Tuesday. These are the ones that do.
hb2.what-we-believe.1: One clear way beats five configurable ones
hb2.what-we-believe.2: Every option we add is something you have to read, understand and decide about. We would rather make a good choice for you and tell you what it is. That is why the dashboard has few switches, why the API has one way to send a message, and why the documentation shows the shortest path first.
hb2.what-we-believe.4: A feature is on the website when it works, not when it is planned. If something is limited, we write the limit next to it. If something does not exist yet, we do not hint that it does. You can plan around a promise only if the promise is true.
hb2.what-we-believe.6: We keep message content and logs only for the retention period of your plan, then delete them. We do not sell your data and we do not read your messages for advertising. Access to stored mail is limited to operating the service and answering a support request you opened.
hb2.what-we-believe.8: We are a small team, and we use that. Decisions are made by the people who will live with them, a bug report can reach the person who can fix it the same day, and nobody has to ask for a meeting to change a sentence on a page. We try to stay this way as long as the service allows.
hb2.how-we-got-here.lead: Geserd was not planned as an email company. It became one by rebuilding the same thing until it was right.
hb2.how-we-got-here.2: The service began as a rebuild of an earlier project that was built around Telegram bots. That project had users, accounts and a sending pipeline, but the shape was wrong for what people actually needed. We kept the lessons, threw away the shape and started again with one goal: a service where you register, add your own domain, prove it is yours, send from it, and receive and reply on the same address.
hb2.how-we-got-here.4.0: Verification is the product. Most of the pain in email lives in DNS. Showing exactly which record is missing, and checking it again for you, matters more than any extra feature.
hb2.how-we-got-here.4.1: Logs are a feature, not a luxury. When something fails you want the whole story: when it was accepted, when it was handed on, what the other side replied.
hb2.how-we-got-here.4.2: Region matters. People in different countries face different rules about where their data may live and how they may sign in, so the service has to know where you are and adapt.
hb2.how-we-got-here.6: Today Geserd runs on servers we operate ourselves, speaks four languages, offers sending and receiving over an HTTP API and over SMTP, and has a public changelog where every visible change is written down. The domain geserd.com is the only official address; if you see the name anywhere else, it is not us.
hb2.how-we-got-here.7: There is a lot left to build. The point of writing this down is to be honest that the road was not straight, and that we expect it to bend again.
hb2.how-we-make-money.lead: We charge for sending and receiving email. That is the whole business model, and it shapes how we treat you.
hb2.how-we-make-money.2: There are four plans: Free, Pro, Business and Enterprise. Free lets you try the whole service on one domain with low limits, so you can see that mail really arrives before you pay anything. Pro and Business raise the daily and monthly limits, the number of domains, keys and webhook endpoints, and how long logs are kept. Enterprise is for custom limits and a contract.
hb2.how-we-make-money.3: Prices are shown in the currency of your region: roubles for visitors from Russia and neighbouring countries, another currency elsewhere, converted by the exchange rate. The number you see is the number you pay.
hb2.how-we-make-money.5.0: Your data. It is not a product and never becomes one.
hb2.how-we-make-money.5.1: Your attention. There are no advertising cookies on the site. Counting visits and clicks runs only with your consent and is not shared with third parties.
hb2.how-we-make-money.5.2: Surprises. If a limit changes, if a price changes, you hear about it before it applies to you.
hb2.how-we-make-money.6: Why this model is good for you
hb2.how-we-make-money.7: When revenue comes only from delivered mail, our interests line up with yours. We earn when your messages arrive, we lose when they do not, and the cheapest way to keep earning is to be reliable, plain and fair. We also support companies working in specific regions with a dedicated tariff on its own page, because a rate that suits a large company in one country can be out of reach for a small business in another.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.t: How we talk to each other
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.lead: Clear writing is a kindness. Most of how we work together comes down to writing things down so that nobody has to guess.
title.handbook.company.how-we-talk-to-ea: How we talk to each other — Geserd
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.2: A decision that lives in someone’s head is a decision that will be made again, differently. When we decide something that affects the service, the site or a customer, it goes into the project notes, with the reason. The next person, or the same person three months later, reads the reason and does not have to rediscover it.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.4.0: Answer the question first. The reply starts with the answer, then the explanation, never the other way round.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.4.1: Use your language. The site, the dashboard and the emails follow the language you picked. Support replies in the language you wrote in when we can.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.4.2: Say what we do not know. “We are checking” is a real answer when it is true, followed by what we will check and when you will hear back.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.5: How we write in the product
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.6: Buttons say what they do. Errors say what went wrong and what to try next, in words rather than codes. Empty screens explain what will appear and how to make it appear. We avoid exclamation marks, jokes at your expense and the word “simply”: if something were simple you would not be reading the sentence.
hb2.how-we-talk-to-each-other.8: We argue about the work, not the person, and we argue with evidence: a screenshot, a log line, a number. When a disagreement stays open, the person who will maintain the result decides, writes the reason down, and we revisit it if the facts change.
hb2.our-tech-stack.lead: We pick boring, well understood tools and spend our effort on the parts that are specific to email.
title.handbook.engineering.our-tech-stac: What is our tech stack — Geserd
hb2.our-tech-stack.2: Geserd has two parts. The website, the documentation and the dashboard are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript served as static files. The API behind them is a Node.js application using Express, with PostgreSQL for data. There is no front-end framework to update and no build step that can break on a Friday: what you read in the repository is what the browser receives.
hb2.our-tech-stack.4: Outgoing and incoming mail goes through a mail server we run ourselves, not through another provider’s sending service. We sign every message with DKIM, publish SPF and DMARC for our own domain, and keep the reverse DNS name of the server consistent with the name it introduces itself with. The same server accepts SMTP submission on ports 465 and 587, where the password is simply an API key, so older applications can connect without code changes.
hb2.our-tech-stack.6.0: Fewer moving parts means fewer 3 a.m. surprises. Every dependency we add is a thing that can break, be abandoned or ship a vulnerability.
hb2.our-tech-stack.6.1: One person can hold it in their head. A system you can read from top to bottom is a system you can fix quickly.
hb2.our-tech-stack.6.2: Speed is a feature. Static pages and a small API are fast without clever tricks.
hb2.our-tech-stack.7: When a new need arrives, the question is not “which tool is fashionable” but “what is the least we must add to meet it”.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.lead: Every change you can see or feel is written down in the public changelog. Shipping is a habit, not an event.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.2: A page is not finished when it looks right on one screen. Before a change ships we look at it on a phone-width and a desktop-width screen, in the dark and the light theme, and in more than one language. We run automated checks that find text left untranslated, layout that overflows sideways, and style names that collide with existing ones. If a check fails, the change waits.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.4.0: Write it. The change and the reason go into the project notes before the code.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.4.1: Build it small. One change at a time, so that if something is wrong we know which one.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.4.2: Test it. The API has automated tests; pages are checked in the browser at real sizes.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.4.3: Update the server. One command pulls the site, another the API, and the service restarts only when it must.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.4.4: Record it. A dated line in the changelog tells you what changed, in all four languages.
hb2.how-we-ship-changes.6: We prefer many small releases to one large one. A small release is easy to explain, easy to check and easy to take back. When a change touches how mail is sent, we treat it more carefully than a change to a page, because a mistake there reaches your customers rather than just your screen.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.lead: Problems are posted on the status page as they happen, with their impact and what we are doing. Silence is the worst update.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.2: An incident is anything that stops mail from being accepted, sent or received as it should, anything that makes the dashboard or the API unavailable, and anything that puts your data at risk. Slow is also a kind of broken: if sending takes much longer than usual, that is an incident even though nothing has failed outright.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.4.0: Say it first. A short note goes on the status page as soon as we are sure something is wrong, even before we know why.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.4.1: Stop the damage. We reduce the impact before we hunt for the root cause.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.4.2: Keep updating. Even “still working on it” is posted, so nobody wonders whether we noticed.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.4.3: Close it plainly. When it is fixed we say what broke, what you may need to resend, and what we change so it does not repeat.
hb2.how-we-handle-incidents.6: After a serious incident we write down the timeline and the causes. We look for the gap in the system that allowed a person to make a mistake, not for the person. The fix is usually a check, a safer default or a clearer message, and it goes into the changelog like any other change.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.lead: Protection is a list of small, unglamorous habits applied everywhere, not one clever feature.
title.handbook.engineering.how-we-protec: How we protect your data — Geserd
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.2: An API key is shown to you once, when you create it. We store only a one-way hash of it, which means that we cannot show it again and nobody who reads our database can use it. If you lose a key, you create a new one and delete the old one. Sign-in uses one-time codes by email or a provider you already trust, so there is no password of ours to leak.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.4: Everything between your browser or application and our servers travels over TLS, and plain HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS. Mail is sent to other servers with encryption whenever the receiving server offers it. Stored message content is kept only for as long as your plan says, then deleted: one day on Free, seven on Pro, thirty on Business, and custom on Enterprise.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.6.0: You see everything in your account: domains, keys, logs and message content within retention.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.6.1: We open stored mail only to operate the service or to answer a request that you opened.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.6.2: Nobody else does: no advertising partners, no analytics vendors, no resale.
hb2.how-we-protect-your-data.8: You pick an account region when you register, because rules about where data may be stored differ between countries. Some sign-in methods are unavailable in some regions for the same reason, and the sign-in pages say so. We would rather tell you about a limit than let you find it by accident.
hb2.how-we-help-users.lead: Good support is mostly fast, honest and specific. We try to be all three, in your language, on the channel you already have open.
hb2.how-we-help-users.2: The fastest route is a ticket opened from the dashboard, because it already knows who you are, which domain you mean and what your recent messages did. A ticket works like a conversation: you write, we reply, and you see the whole thread in one place on your phone or your computer. If you are not signed in, the contact page reaches the same team.
hb2.how-we-help-users.4.0: It names the cause. “Your DKIM record is missing a character” beats “check your DNS”.
hb2.how-we-help-users.4.1: It gives the next step. One concrete action, not a list of ten possibilities.
hb2.how-we-help-users.4.2: It does not blame you. Most email problems are traps that anyone could fall into.
hb2.how-we-help-users.6: When your question is answered the ticket is closed, and a closed ticket stays as a record you can read but not continue. A new question gets a new ticket, so each thread stays about one thing and is easy to find later. Before you open one, the help page and the documentation answer the most common questions in a few lines, and the status page tells you whether the problem is on our side.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.lead: Bug reports and rough edges are the most useful thing you can send us. They are how the service gets better.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.2: Feedback is a topic when you open a ticket, so it reaches the people who read tickets rather than disappearing into a form. Say what you tried, what you expected and what happened. A screenshot or the text of an error is worth a paragraph. You do not need to propose a solution; describing the problem well is already most of the work.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.4.0: We reproduce it. If we can see the problem ourselves, it moves from a report to a task.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.4.1: We fix what is small, now. A typo, a clipped label or a wrong colour is repaired the same day.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.4.2: We write down what is large. Bigger requests go into the plan with the reason they matter, and when they ship they appear in the changelog.
hb2.how-we-use-feedback.5: We cannot promise to build everything we are asked for. We do promise that a report is read, that you get an honest answer, and that we will tell you when a thing you reported has been fixed.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.t: What is our philosophy for anti-abuse
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.lead: Every sender shares the same reputation with the world’s mail servers. One abuser can make email worse for all of them, so we take it seriously.
title.handbook.success.our-philosophy-on: What is our philosophy for anti-abuse — Geserd
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.2: Mail providers judge a sender by what recipients do: how many report a message as spam, how many addresses do not exist, how many bounce. A service that lets bad mail through sees its good mail filtered too. Protecting deliverability is therefore not a favour to the receiving side; it is the thing you are paying us for.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.4: The acceptable use policy says what is not allowed on Geserd: unsolicited bulk mail, purchased lists, deceptive messages, phishing and anything illegal where you or the recipient live. It is written in plain language and lives on its own page, so nobody can say they were not told.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.6.0: Signals from the mail itself. Bounce rate, complaint rate and unsubscribe rate are tracked for every account and shown to you as a delivery score from 0 to 100, where higher is better.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.6.1: Signals from behaviour. Many accounts created from the same place for the same purpose are a pattern that we look for, because abusers rarely stop at one account.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.6.2: Reports from people. If you receive mail you did not ask for, tell us; every report is read.
hb2.our-philosophy-on-abuse.8: We act in steps that match the problem. A first warning gives you the chance to fix a mistake. A temporary freeze stops sending while we talk. A block ends the account when abuse is clear. Automatic checks propose the step, and a person looks at the evidence and decides, so that an honest mistake is not treated like a campaign. You can always ask why through a ticket and receive an actual reason.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.lead: Design here means making something clear to use, not making it loud. The best interface is the one you stop noticing.
title.handbook.design.how-we-think-about: How we think about design — Geserd
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.2: The site is black, white and shades of grey. Colour is kept for meaning: a state that needs your attention, a brand mark that a provider requires. Without decoration competing for your eye, text and the one action that matters on a page stand out on their own. Headings use a soft fade from white to grey and nothing else; we avoid rainbow effects because they say “look at me” and not “here is what you need”.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.4.0: Every page works on a phone. We check at 390 and 1440 pixels wide, because both are how you really use it.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.4.1: Every language gets the same care. A sentence is not finished until it fits in Russian, French and German too, where words are longer.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.4.2: Both themes are real. The dashboard and the documentation work in dark and light, and neither is an afterthought.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.4.3: Space is part of the design. Sections have room around them; cramped is a bug, not a style.
hb2.how-we-think-about-design.6: Animation is used to show what is happening, not to decorate: a check that draws itself when a record is verified, a bar that grows as a score is calculated, a panel that slides from the edge it belongs to. Every animation is short, and the ones that could bother you turn off if your system asks for reduced motion.
hb2.brand-guidelines.lead: A brand is a promise that looks the same everywhere. These rules keep Geserd recognisable, and keep you safe from lookalikes.
title.handbook.design.brand-guidelines: What are our brand guidelines — Geserd
hb2.brand-guidelines.2: The name is written Geserd, with a capital G and the rest in lowercase, in every language and in every sentence. It is never split, abbreviated or turned into a verb. The only official web address is geserd.com. If a message, a site or a profile uses the name with a different domain, it is not ours, and we would like to hear about it.
hb2.brand-guidelines.4.0: The wordmark is the full name set in our own letters, used on the site, in the footer and in emails. It is white on black and black on white, nothing else.
hb2.brand-guidelines.4.1: The icon is the single letter G, used where space is tight, such as the browser tab.
hb2.brand-guidelines.4.2: Do not stretch, recolour, outline, rotate, add shadows or place the logo on a busy picture.
hb2.brand-guidelines.6: Black, white and greys carry almost everything. Text is set in a clean sans-serif; headings may use a calm serif when a page wants more weight. Shapes are generous: cards and panels have large rounded corners, controls are pill-shaped or softly rounded, and buttons that matter use a frosted glass look. Icons are drawn with one line weight, in one style, and never as arrows or paper planes, which every email product already uses.
hb2.brand-guidelines.8: You may say that you use Geserd, and show the logo to say so, for example “Sent with Geserd” or in a list of tools. Do not suggest that we endorse, sponsor or are partnered with you without our written agreement, and do not use the name in your own product or domain name. If you are unsure, ask through a ticket and we will answer.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.lead: A spam folder is not a punishment. It is a guess made by a mailbox provider from a handful of signals, and most of them are in your hands.
title.handbook.mail.why-mail-lands-in-sp: Why mail lands in spam — Geserd
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.2: Every receiving server answers one question: do I trust this message? It looks at who sent it, whether that sender proved who they are, how recipients treated earlier mail from the same sender, and what the message itself looks like. No single signal decides. Together they decide whether you land in the inbox, in the spam folder, or nowhere at all.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.4: SPF says which servers may send for your domain, DKIM signs each message so it cannot be altered unnoticed, and DMARC tells the receiver what to do when a check fails. Geserd generates the exact records for each domain you add. If any of them is missing or wrong, your mail starts with a handicap that no wording can fix.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.6: Providers remember. A sender whose mail is opened and answered earns trust; a sender whose mail is reported as spam, or sent to addresses that do not exist, loses it. A new domain has no history, so it starts cautiously. Send small, steady volumes at first and grow them over a few weeks instead of sending everything on day one.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.8.0: A clear sender name that recipients recognise, and a From address on your own domain.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.8.1: A plain-text version next to the HTML, and real text rather than one big image.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.8.2: A short, honest subject line without capital letters, repeated exclamation marks or promises you do not keep.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.8.3: An unsubscribe link in every newsletter. Geserd adds one automatically to broadcasts.
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.9: How to find out what went wrong
hb2.why-mail-lands-in-spam.10: Start with the delivery score on the Metrics page and the event log of the message. A message that was delivered but not seen is a reputation or content problem. A message that bounced is an address problem. A message that never left is a domain or limit problem, and the log says which. The guide on spam and bounces below explains what to do next.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.lead: Three numbers describe the health of your sending: how many messages bounce, how many are reported as spam, and how close you are to your limits. This is what each one means and what to do about it.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.1: Bounces: the address is the problem
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.2: A hard bounce means the address does not exist or refuses mail for good. Geserd stops sending to it automatically, because writing to dead addresses is the fastest way to look like a bought list. A soft bounce is temporary, such as a full mailbox or a busy server, so Geserd retries with growing pauses before it gives up.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.3.0: Keep the bounce rate under 2 percent. Above that, providers start to doubt the list.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.3.1: Check addresses when people sign up. A typo caught at the form is a bounce avoided.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.3.2: Never re-add suppressed addresses. The suppression list exists to protect you.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.4: Complaints: the person is the problem
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.5: A complaint happens when a recipient presses the spam button instead of unsubscribing. Providers weigh it far more than a bounce, because the mail arrived and a real person still did not want it. Geserd records each complaint, stops sending to that address and lowers the conduct part of your account rating. Aim for well under 0.1 percent.
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.6: Limits: why they exist and how they behave
hb2.bounces-complaints-limits.7: Each plan has a daily and a monthly sending limit. They protect the shared reputation of the service and keep a bug in your code from sending ten thousand messages by accident. When a limit is reached, new sends are refused with a clear error before anything is queued, and a running broadcast pauses and continues by itself when the period resets. You get a notice at 80 percent so it never comes as a surprise.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.lead: Everyone who sends through Geserd shares the same standing with the mail servers of the world. That is why we check mail on the way out, watch behaviour, and act early.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.2: Every outgoing message gets a spam score from a set of readable rules: shouting subjects, hidden text, link shorteners, missing text part, suspicious attachments and similar patterns. In the sending settings you choose how strict we are: off, balanced or strict. A rejected message is never sent and does not count against your limits, and the response tells you which rules fired so you can fix the text.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.4: Spammers rarely stop at one account. We look at patterns around accounts: many registrations from one place in a short time, the same browser behind several accounts, the same tax number in several applications, disposable email domains. These raise a flag. A flag is not a verdict: a person reviews the evidence before anything permanent happens, so an honest mistake is never treated like a campaign.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.6.0: A warning. You hear about the problem first and get the chance to fix it.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.6.1: A freeze. Sending stops while we talk, but you can still use the dashboard and write to support.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.6.2: A block. Used only when abuse is clear. You are told why, and you can ask a person to look again.
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.7: What you can do to stay clear
hb2.how-we-fight-spam.8: Send only to people who expect your mail, honour unsubscribes the same day, keep one account per organisation and keep your delivery score high. The acceptable use policy lists the rules in plain language, and the account rating on your profile shows how Geserd sees your sending right now.
hb2.single-sign-on.lead: With single sign-on your team opens Geserd with the company account they already use. No new password, and access ends the moment a person leaves the company.
hb2.single-sign-on.2: Single sign-on is part of the Enterprise plan and is set up by our team under your contract. It fits companies that already run an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta, Keycloak or any service that speaks OpenID Connect.
hb2.single-sign-on.4.0: Your colleague enters a work email on the sign-in page. Geserd recognises the company domain.
hb2.single-sign-on.4.1: They are sent to your provider and sign in there, with your password rules and your second factor.
hb2.single-sign-on.4.2: Your provider confirms who they are. Geserd checks the signature, the audience and that the email belongs to your domain.
hb2.single-sign-on.4.3: They land in the dashboard. The first time, Geserd creates the account; later it recognises it.
hb2.single-sign-on.6: Register a new application in your identity provider, with the redirect address we give you, and send us four things: the company email domain, the issuer address, the client ID and the client secret. We check the connection before we turn it on. The secret is stored encrypted and is never shown again, not even to our own staff.
hb2.single-sign-on.8.0: One domain, one provider. Each company domain points to one connection, which we can turn off at any moment.
hb2.single-sign-on.8.1: Verified email only. If your provider does not confirm the address, sign-in is refused.
hb2.single-sign-on.8.2: Offboarding is yours. Disable the person in your provider and they cannot sign in again.
doc.mp.concepts.lead: The handful of ideas that explain everything else in Geserd: domains, keys, emails, events and limits.
doc.mp.concepts.2: A domain is the address you send from, such as mail.yourshop.com. Geserd generates a DKIM key pair for it and shows the DNS records that prove you control it. Until the records are verified, the domain is in the sandbox and can send only to your own account address.
doc.mp.concepts.4: A key lets your code talk to the API. It is shown once, stored only as a hash, and can be revoked at any time. Create separate keys for separate apps so that revoking one never breaks the others.
doc.mp.concepts.6: Sending returns an id immediately and the message is queued. It then moves through states: sent, delivered, or bounced and complained when something goes wrong. Every step is written to the event log and, if you set up a webhook, pushed to your server.
doc.mp.concepts.8.0: Events describe what happened to a message, for example email.delivered.
doc.mp.concepts.8.1: Webhooks deliver events to your server, signed so you can trust them.
doc.mp.concepts.8.2: Limits cap sending per day and per month on every plan.
doc.mp.going-live.lead: Ten minutes of checks before you send to real customers saves days of cleaning up reputation later.
doc.mp.going-live.2.0: The domain is verified. Domains shows SPF, DKIM and MX as verified, not pending.
doc.mp.going-live.2.1: DMARC exists. Start with p=none and a report address, then tighten it after a few weeks.
doc.mp.going-live.2.2: The From address is real. Replies go somewhere a person reads.
doc.mp.going-live.2.3: Keys are in environment variables, never in the repository or in front-end code.
doc.mp.going-live.2.4: A webhook is listening for email.bounced and email.complained, so you stop writing to bad addresses.
doc.mp.going-live.4: Start with a small, steady volume and increase it every day. Watch the delivery score on Metrics and the event log. If bounces climb above two percent, pause and clean the list before sending more.
doc.mp.going-live.5: The handbook article on why mail lands in spam explains every signal in more detail.
doc.mp.node.lead: Send your first email from Node.js 18 or newer with the built-in `fetch`. No library is required.
doc.mp.node.3: Keep the key in an environment variable named GESERD_KEY. The response contains the message id, which you can look up in the Logs page or through GET /api/emails/:id.
doc.mp.node.5: Retry only on 429 and 5xx, with a growing pause. A 4xx other than 429 means the request itself must change, so repeating it will not help. Use an idempotency key if a retry could otherwise send the same message twice.
doc.mp.python.lead: Send email from Python with the standard `urllib` or with the `requests` package.
doc.mp.python.3: Always set a timeout. A request without one can hang a worker forever when the network misbehaves.
doc.mp.python.5: If your app already speaks SMTP, point it at the SMTP settings shown on the SMTP page of your dashboard, with your API key as the password. No code change is needed beyond the host, port and credentials.
doc.mp.php.lead: Send email from plain PHP with cURL, for example from a contact form or a small shop.
doc.mp.php.3: On shared hosting, set the key in the control panel as an environment variable or in a file outside the web root. Never put it in a file that the site serves.
doc.mp.receive-reply.lead: Receive mail sent to your domain and answer it from the same address.
doc.mp.receive-reply.2: Add the MX record shown for your domain at your DNS provider. If the domain already receives mail somewhere else, use a subdomain such as inbox.yourshop.com so the two never compete.
doc.mp.receive-reply.6: Reply by sending a normal email with in_reply_to set to the id of the received message. Geserd adds the threading headers, so the answer appears in the same conversation in the customer’s mailbox.
doc.mp.emails.lead: Send a message, check it before sending, and read its status.
doc.mp.emails.2: POST /api/emails queues a message and answers 202 with its id. The from address must be on a verified domain.
doc.mp.emails.3.r0: Sender, on a verified domain. Required.
doc.mp.emails.3.r1: One address or a list. Required.
doc.mp.emails.3.r3: HTML body. Send html, text or both.
doc.mp.emails.3.r4: Plain-text body. Recommended next to html.
doc.mp.emails.3.r6: Id of a received message, to answer it in the same thread.
doc.mp.emails.3.r7: Files to attach, as a list.
doc.mp.emails.5: POST /api/emails/check accepts the same body and returns the spam score and the rules that fired, without sending anything or using your limits.
doc.mp.emails.7: GET /api/emails lists recent messages and GET /api/emails/:id returns one message with its status and events.
doc.mp.domains.lead: Add a domain, read the DNS records it needs, verify it and remove it.
doc.mp.domains.1.r1: Add a domain by its name.
doc.mp.domains.1.r2: Status and the DNS records to publish.
doc.mp.domains.3: After adding a domain, publish the returned records and call verify. DNS can take from a few minutes to a few hours to spread, so a pending status right after publishing is normal. Verification can be repeated as often as you like.
doc.mp.domains.4: Your plan limits how many domains you can add. Past the limit the API answers 403 plan_limit.
doc.mp.api-keys.lead: Create, list and revoke keys, and send them correctly with every request.
doc.mp.api-keys.3: Send the key as a bearer token on every request over HTTPS. A request without a valid key answers 401 unauthorized.
doc.mp.api-keys.5.r0: List keys. Secrets are never returned.
doc.mp.api-keys.5.r1: Create a key. The secret is shown once.
doc.mp.api-keys.6: If a key leaks, revoke it first and investigate afterwards. A revoked key stops working at once, and creating a replacement takes seconds.
doc.mp.webhooks.lead: Receive events on your server and verify that they really come from Geserd.
doc.mp.webhooks.2.r5: The message could not be sent.
doc.mp.webhooks.4: Each request carries three headers: Geserd-Id, Geserd-Timestamp and Geserd-Signature. The signature is v1= followed by the hex HMAC-SHA256 of id.timestamp.body using your webhook secret. Compare it in constant time and reject requests whose timestamp is more than five minutes old.
doc.mp.webhooks.7: Answer with any 2xx status within ten seconds. Other answers are retried with growing pauses. Webhook addresses that resolve to private networks are refused, so use a public HTTPS address.
doc.mp.templates.lead: Store a message once and send it many times with variables.
doc.mp.templates.1.r2: Edit a template. Saves a version.
doc.mp.templates.2: Every edit saves a version, so you can see what changed and return to an earlier text. Use preview before you send, and the test endpoint to see the message in a real mailbox.
doc.mp.idempotency.lead: Make a retry safe: the same request sent twice must not produce two emails.
doc.mp.idempotency.2: A network can fail after the server accepted your request but before you saw the answer. Retrying then sends the message twice. For a password reset that is annoying; for an invoice it is a problem.
doc.mp.idempotency.4.0: Generate one unique value for each logical message, for example the order id plus the message type.
doc.mp.idempotency.4.1: Store the id Geserd returned. Before retrying, look it up in GET /api/emails/:id instead of sending again.
doc.mp.idempotency.4.2: Keep a record in your own database that the message was requested, so a restarted worker does not repeat it.
doc.mp.security.lead: What Geserd does to protect your account and your mail, and what stays in your hands.
doc.mp.security.2.0: API keys are stored only as hashes and shown once.
doc.mp.security.2.1: Webhook requests are signed, and secrets can be rotated at any time.
doc.mp.security.2.2: Sign-in supports authenticator-app codes as a second factor.
doc.mp.security.2.3: Secrets for company sign-in are stored encrypted and never shown again.
doc.mp.security.4.0: Keep keys out of repositories and front-end code.
doc.mp.security.4.1: Use one key per application and revoke the ones you no longer use.
doc.mp.security.4.2: Verify webhook signatures before you trust a payload.
doc.mp.security.4.3: Turn on two-factor sign-in for every person with access.
doc.mp.security.5: To report a vulnerability, open a ticket from the Help page with the topic “Security”. We answer these first.
doc.mp.glossary.lead: Short answers to the words you will meet in email setup.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r0: Which servers may send for the domain.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r1: A signature proving a message was not altered.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r2: What receivers do when SPF or DKIM fail.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r3: The record that says where incoming mail goes.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r4: Reverse DNS: the name behind a server address.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r5: A message that could not be delivered.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r6: A recipient marked the message as spam.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r7: Addresses we no longer write to.
doc.mp.glossary.1.r8: The mode before a domain is verified.
doc.mp.glossary.2: The beginners section explains SPF, DKIM, DMARC and DNS records in plain words, with screenshots of where to click at the most common domain companies.
